extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and readers seeking criteria to evaluate or improve poetic composition (particularly lyric/epic poetry)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria for judging and composing poetry — covering diction, imagery, characterization, form, tone, and moral/ philosophical balance, illustrated via criticism of Wordsworth. Useful for poets and critics assessing poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contextual incongruity of diction
rubrics_metrics.description: “the feeling of incongruity is seldom excited by the diction of any passage considered in itself, but by the sudden superiority of some other passage forming the context.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure diction across a poem is consistent in quality and tone so no passage unexpectedly outshines or jars with its neighbors. Watch for local phrases that are fine alone but create a sense of mismatch when set beside surrounding lines; edit to preserve a coherent register across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid laborious minuteness in local imagery (matter-of-factness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objection to a 'matter-of-factness' consisting of laborious minuteness and fidelity in representation of objects and their positions, and insertion of accidental circumstances to explain characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-describe small local details that a painter or draughtsman could show more economically; avoid episodic, documentary detail that forces the reader to assemble a picture piece-by-piece. Prefer imagery that invokes the imagination and generality rather than exhaustive, map-like particulars. Example: long descriptive plates in THE EXCURSION that could have been left to a visual artist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paint to the imagination, not to the fancy (create whole images)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should 'paint to the imagination, not to the fancy' — aiming at creation rather than piecemeal painting, giving the whole picture flashed at once upon the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for images that present a co-presence of the whole scene (a sudden imaginative flash) rather than assembling parts laboriously. Use language that evokes multiple senses and associative 'vestigia communia' so a single phrase summons a rich, unified perception (Milton praised as exemplar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid biographical over-explanation of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Minute adherence to matter-of-fact in character and incidents: a biographical attention to probability and an anxiety of explanation and retrospect which is superfluous in poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters in poetry should remain representative rather than exhaustively biographical. Resist inventing detailed backstories to justify a character's traits in the poem; excessive explanation breaks the poetic illusion and can make fiction feel false rather than fictitious. Horace's precepts invoked: prudent restraint in particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose characters appropriate to poetic ends (representative dignity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenge to critics who question choice of 'mean' characters; poet's aim may be to exhibit human dignity across ranks. But also an objection: some objects belong to moral philosophy rather than elevated poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting characters (including humble figures), ensure their presence serves poetic ends (pleasure, imagination, universal feeling) and does not reduce poetry to sermonizing. If using low-rank figures, do not overload the poem with justificatory anecdotes — the character should embody representative qualities intelligible to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's immediate object should be pleasure (avoid direct didacticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: It 'seems... to destroy the main fundamental distinction... between a poem and prose' if poetry's immediate object is truth rather than pleasure; poetry must use pleasure as the means to moralize readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making poetry a straightforward vehicle for philosophical or sermonic argument. Use aesthetic pleasure as the primary aim; moral or intellectual aims should follow from and be mediated by the reader's enjoyment of the poem, not replace it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attribute implausible powers to characters via forced biography
rubrics_metrics.description: Objection to inventing accounts of birth, parentage, education, and lucky accidents to make an improbable character (e.g., a chimney-sweeper who is poet and philosopher) credible; 'Nothing, but biography, can justify this.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character possesses extraordinary gifts, do not rely on contrived life-histories within the poem to justify them; either alter the character type to one naturally fitting those gifts (e.g., make him a poet), or accept the fictional status without attempting false historicity, otherwise the fiction feels 'false.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid undue predilection for dramatic form that creates voice problems
rubrics_metrics.description: An undue predilection for the dramatic form can lead to: (a) thoughts and diction different from the poet (incongruity of style), or (b) the same voice indistinguishable across characters (ventriloquism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting dramatic speech, ensure distinct, believable voices for characters and avoid letting the poet's own diction simply masquerade as multiple speakers. If characters' speech is not sufficiently differentiated, the drama becomes a ventriloquist effect—two characters represented but only one true voice present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disproportionate intensity of feeling (prolixity & repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defect: intensity of feeling disproportionate to the knowledge and value of the objects described, producing occasional prolixity, repetition, and an eddying instead of progression of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the emotional intensity to the material and the average reader's anticipatable sympathy; avoid overlong elaboration, repeated motifs without forward movement, and circular trains of thought that stall the poem's progression. Examples cited: specific pages/lines in THE EXCURSION.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid thoughts and images too great for the subject (mental bombast)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disproportion of thought to the circumstance and occasion—'thoughts and images too great for the subject'—resulting in mental bombast (not verbal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the scale of philosophical or visionary statements appropriate to the occasion depicted. Grand, metaphysical thoughts should be reserved for subjects that warrant them; otherwise the effect is awkwardly inflated and can feel like misapplied genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain tonal consistency; avoid abrupt fall from sublime to trivial
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrated by abrupt sinking from a sublime couplet ('They flash upon that inward eye...') to a light, trivial final line ('And then my heart with pleasure fills, And dances with the daffodils.') — such shifts can be burlesque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure transitions in tone are handled so that the sublime and the comic/pastoral do not collide jarringly; preserve an arc so the reader isn't jolted from exaltation to banality. Rework lines that create a medley-like drop in tonal register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incoherent metaphysical attributions (meaning must cohere)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of attributing magnificent attributes (Prophet, Seer, Immortality brooding) to a six-year-old child without clarity—either these claims are absurd in common sense, or they must be reinterpreted into trivial truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure metaphors and metaphysical claims have coherent referents; do not force paradoxical or mystical attributions that would require miracles or impossibilities to be true. If using grand metaphors for ordinary subjects, supply a consistent logic or risk making words either meaningless or banal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Austere purity and precision of language (grammatical & logical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Praised: an 'austere purity of language both grammatically and logically; in short a perfect appropriateness of the words to the meaning.' The infallible test: untranslatableness without injury to meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for exact, appropriate word choice that carries both denotation and the intended associative overtones. Avoid vitiated modern phrases, affected diction, and loose logic. Teach careful attention to each word's meaning and place; the ideal is diction so apt it resists translation without loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original, weighty, and meditative thoughts (freshness from observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellence: 'a correspondent weight and sanity of the Thoughts and Sentiments,—won, not from books; but—from the poet’s own meditative observation.' Lines should be fresh and 'native.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate original reflections arising from personal, contemplative engagement with experience rather than learned platitudes. Valued qualities: seriousness, sanity, freshness, and meditative insight that remain striking under analysis. Shorter poems should still contain just, original reflections.
